summary: Defines how a WebRTC data channel is used to carry CLUE protocol messages between two CLUE entities. This gives telepresence endpoints a reliable path for their control messages alongside the media. It is an experimental document.

eli5.summary: Besides sending pictures and sound, video rooms must pass little notes to each other. This document says how to use a built-in message lane in a WebRTC connection to carry those notes.

subtitle: How telepresence endpoints exchange control messages over WebRTC.

tldr.problem: Telepresence endpoints need a reliable path to exchange control messages about which video and audio streams to send and receive. The main media streams are not suitable for this delicate signaling.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8850 specifies that CLUE (Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence) protocol messages travel over a WebRTC data channel, which uses SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) over DTLS encryption for ordered, reliable delivery.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can now coordinate complex multi-stream telepresence sessions with guaranteed message delivery. The RFC is experimental, published in January 2021.

today: RFC 8850 remains an Experimental specification published in January 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
CLUE (Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence) is a protocol that lets endpoints negotiate which video and audio streams to send and receive in complex telepresence conferences. RFC 8847 defines CLUE itself; this RFC defines how to transport CLUE messages reliably between endpoints.

The RFC specifies using WebRTC data channels, which are bidirectional SCTP streams carried over DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security). This provides ordered, reliable delivery of CLUE control messages alongside the media streams. The document also explains how to negotiate and describe the data channel using the Session Description Protocol (SDP) in the offer/answer model.
sections.eli5: Telepresence rooms send control notes over a special message lane in WebRTC. This section says what that lane is and why it is needed.

sections.title: The CLUE Data Channel
sections.content:
The CLUE data channel is built on top of WebRTC data channels as defined in RFC 8831. It uses a pair of SCTP streams (one in each direction) within a single SCTP association carried over DTLS. Both streams must use the same SCTP stream identifier value.

Within a CLUE session, each entity must use a single CLUE data channel for all CLUE messages to its peer. The data channel uses PPID (SCTP Payload Protocol Identifier) value 51, which indicates UTF-8 encoded text.

Key SCTP settings for a CLUE data channel are: ordered delivery (messages arrive in sequence), full reliability (no partial reliability extensions are allowed), and support for stream reset (RFC 6525). These settings ensure CLUE control messages always arrive in order and in full.
sections.eli5: The data channel is two one-way streets: one for sending, one for receiving. Messages are always ordered and complete. The channel can be reset if needed.

sections.title: SDP Negotiation
sections.content:
Endpoints negotiate the CLUE data channel using SDP (Session Description Protocol) in the offer/answer model, as defined in RFC 3264. The SDP media description uses the application media type with UDP/DTLS/SCTP or TCP/DTLS/SCTP proto values and webrtc-datachannel format.

The SDP must include a sctp-port attribute specifying the SCTP port, and a dcmap (data channel mapping) attribute specifying the SCTP stream ID, subprotocol (set to CLUE), and that the channel is ordered with full reliability. An example shows: m=application 54111 UDP/DTLS/SCTP webrtc-datachannel, a=sctp-port: 5000, and a=dcmap:2 subprotocol="CLUE";ordered=true.

Endpoints SHOULD prefer UDP/DTLS/SCTP unless the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) process determines that TCP is required (for instance, in networks blocking UDP).
sections.eli5: Before sending CLUE messages, endpoints swap notes about which port and settings to use. These notes are written in a format called SDP.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The CLUE data channel relies on the security properties of WebRTC data channels, which include DTLS encryption of all traffic. Since CLUE sessions are typically established using SIP (Session Initiation Protocol), endpoints MUST authenticate each other and authorize the session using SIP mechanisms defined in RFC 3261 before establishing the data channel.

DTLS provides confidentiality and integrity protection for the CLUE messages, preventing eavesdropping and tampering. The combination of SIP authentication and DTLS encryption ensures that only authorized endpoints can receive CLUE messages from their peer.
sections.eli5: Messages sent over the data channel are locked with encryption so nobody can spy on them or change them. Only the right endpoints get the unlock key.
